name: Prime Editing (2019)
teaser: David Liu's lab unveiled 'prime editing' — a CRISPR-derived tool that can make precise edits of any kind, from single-letter changes to insertions and deletions, with far fewer off-target errors than the original. Called a 'word processor' for the genome, it may make the first generation of gene therapies far safer.

exploreAction.targetName: The 2019 Nature paper on prime editing
exploreAction.instruction: Read how prime editing pairs a Cas9 nickase with a reverse transcriptase to copy an edit directly into the genome — no double-strand break needed. The paper's diagrams are worth studying: the 'pegRNA' is the instruction tape. It's CRISPR, but precise enough to fix single disease mutations.

name: CAR-T Cell Therapy (2010s)
teaser: The first 'living drug': doctors harvest a patient's T-cells, re-engineer them to recognize cancer, and infuse them back — where they multiply and hunt tumors. The first pediatric ALL patient, Emily Whitehead, was treated in 2012 when all else failed. CAR-T is now approved for several blood cancers.

exploreAction.targetName: The story of Emily Whitehead and the first CAR-T treatments
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Emily, 6, was hours from death when her doctors infused engineered T-cells — and how she nearly died of the immune storm before recovering. Then how the field scaled: six-figure prices, solid tumors still hard, but blood cancers now curable in many who had no other option. The immune system, weaponized with scissors and glue.

name: Lithium for Mania (1949)
teaser: John Cade, an Australian psychiatrist with a simple lab, injected lithium into guinea pigs, then gave it to patients with manic excitement — with astonishing results. Lithium became the first effective treatment for bipolar disorder, a salt that steadies moods. Cade's paper was 10 pages; it changed psychiatry forever.

exploreAction.targetName: Cade's 1949 paper on lithium salts in mania
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Cade — testing a theory about urine toxins — noticed his guinea pigs calmed under lithium, then tried it on 10 manic patients with dramatic success. The 1950s psychiatrists who dismissed the idea as 'too simple' delayed the field for a decade. A table salt that tames madness.

name: Antidepressants (1950s)
teaser: Iproniazid, a tuberculosis drug, made TB patients in sanatoriums strangely cheerful — the first antidepressant, born as a side effect. Then imipramine, tested as an antipsychotic, proved even more effective. The 'monoamine hypothesis' — depression as a chemistry problem — was born, and still shapes treatment.

exploreAction.targetName: The accidental discovery of the first antidepressants
exploreAction.instruction: Read how sanatorium doctors noticed TB patients on iproniazid dancing and socializing, and how Kline recognized what he was seeing. Then imipramine's story — a failed antipsychotic that lifted mood. The discovery that chemistry can change mood, made twice by accident, transformed mental health care.

name: The Placebo Effect (1955)
teaser: Henry Beecher's 1955 paper 'The Powerful Placebo' assembled evidence that dummy pills relieve real symptoms in roughly a third of patients. The discovery didn't just warn against quackery — it revealed that expectation itself is a physiological force, measurable in brain scans, which modern trials are designed around.

exploreAction.targetName: Beecher's 1955 JAMA paper on the placebo effect
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Beecher, a WWII anesthesiologist who ran out of morphine during the Anzio beachhead, discovered that saline injections relieved pain when soldiers believed they were morphine. His paper made placebo-controlled trials standard. Then read the modern view: nocebo, expectation, and the brain's own pharmacy.

name: Randomized Controlled Trials (1948)
teaser: The first randomized trial — streptomycin for tuberculosis, published in 1948 — assigned patients by a coin-flip-like randomization, blinding assessors, and counting every outcome, including deaths. It set the gold standard for medicine. Before it, doctors trusted anecdotes; after it, they trusted data.

exploreAction.targetName: The 1948 streptomycin trial report
exploreAction.instruction: Read the Medical Research Council's trial: 107 patients, randomized, with X-ray readers who didn't know who got the drug. It seems obvious now; it was radical then. Hill's trial gave the world a method for telling what works from what merely sounds good — the foundation of evidence-based medicine.

name: Smoking Causes Lung Cancer (1950)
teaser: Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill interviewed hundreds of lung cancer patients and controls, and found smokers had massively higher risk — a 1950 case-control study so decisive it ended the debate within a decade. Their 50,000-doctor prospective study confirmed it. The single most important epidemiological discovery of the century.

exploreAction.targetName: Doll & Hill's 1950 BMJ paper on smoking and lung cancer
exploreAction.instruction: Read how the case-control study of 649 patients and 649 controls produced a smoking-lung cancer association so strong that the tobacco industry spent decades denying it. Doll himself, a smoker, quit the day he saw his data and later lived to 92. The study that made 'smoking kills' a fact, not an opinion.

name: Folic Acid Prevents Spina Bifida (1991)
teaser: The MRC's 1991 randomized trial showed that folic acid, taken before conception, prevents most neural tube defects like spina bifida. It's one of the cheapest public health wins ever — a vitamin pill costing pennies, now added to flour in 80+ countries. The discovery that prevention can be baked into bread.

exploreAction.targetName: The 1991 MRC vitamin study results
exploreAction.instruction: Read how the trial recruited women at high risk (previous affected pregnancy) and found a 72% reduction with folic acid. Then the implementation story: mandatory fortification debates, and the countries that quietly added B9 to flour. One vitamin, one decision, thousands of babies spared.

name: Fluoride and Teeth (1930s-40s)
teaser: A Colorado dentist noticed local kids' teeth were stained but strangely decay-free — and the stain tracked to fluoride in the water. Studies confirmed: the right dose of fluoride prevents cavities with no staining. Grand Rapids, Michigan became the first city to fluoridate its water in 1945. Cavities dropped by half within a decade.

exploreAction.targetName: The Grand Rapids fluoridation study
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Dean's 'fluorosis' surveys mapped fluoride levels against cavity rates across hundreds of US cities, finding the sweet spot around 1 ppm. Then the 15-year Grand Rapids trial that settled it. Water fluoridation remains one of the most studied and most contested public health measures — the science is clear, the politics are not.

name: Iodine and Goiter (1917-24)
teaser: The discovery that adding iodine to salt eliminated goiter — the world's first successful mass nutrition intervention. David Marine's trial in Akron, Ohio schoolgirls proved it in 1917, and Michigan adopted iodized salt in 1924. The 'goiter belt' of the American Midwest disappeared within a generation.

exploreAction.targetName: Marine's goiter prevention trial in Akron schoolgirls
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Marine gave iodine to half of 2,000 schoolgirls — a controlled trial before the term existed — and goiter virtually vanished in the treated group. The lesson: a missing mineral can be added to food. Iodized salt is now standard in 120+ countries, one of the cheapest cognitive rescues in history.

name: Beriberi and Rice (1897)
teaser: Christiaan Eijkman noticed that chickens fed polished white rice developed beriberi, while those on unpolished rice stayed healthy — the clue that led to vitamins. He didn't realize the polishings contained a nutrient; he thought a toxin. But his colony of chickens proved that disease could be a diet problem. He won the Nobel in 1929.

exploreAction.targetName: Eijkman's chicken experiment in the Dutch East Indies
exploreAction.instruction: Read how a hospital cook's sudden switch to white rice made Eijkman's lab chickens sick — the accidental experiment that cracked beriberi. He misread it as a poison, and it took Funk to name the missing nutrient. A chicken's diet, a cook's thrift, and the birth of vitamin science.

name: Scurvy and Citrus (1747)
teaser: James Lind, a ship's surgeon, gave twelve scurvy-stricken sailors different remedies — vinegar, seawater, cider, citrus — and the two given oranges and lemons recovered in days. It was the first controlled trial in history, and it solved the disease that had killed more sailors than all wars combined.

exploreAction.targetName: Lind's 1753 Treatise of the Scurvy
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Lind's experiment on the HMS Salisbury divided twelve identical patients into six pairs with six treatments. The citrus pair healed. It still took the Royal Navy 40 years to adopt lemon juice — the difference between a discovery and a policy. The trial that invented clinical testing, and the disease that proved it.

name: Handwashing Saves Lives (1847)
teaser: Ignaz Semmelweis made doctors wash their hands with chlorinated lime between autopsies and deliveries — and maternal mortality at his Vienna clinic plummeted from 18% to 2%. His colleagues rejected the idea and mocked him; he died in an asylum, 14 years before Pasteur proved him right.

exploreAction.targetName: Semmelweis's 1847 handwashing discovery
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Semmelweis connected the terrible statistics of the doctor-run maternity ward to the doctors' habit of coming straight from autopsy. The numbers were undeniable; the medical establishment was not. He published, he argued, he broke down. Germ theory vindicated him after his death. 'Wash your hands' is his monument.

name: The Stethoscope (1816)
teaser: René Laennec, embarrassed to press his ear to a woman's chest, rolled a paper tube instead — and heard her heartbeat better than ever. He spent three years building the wooden monaural stethoscope and mapping its sounds. The symbol of the doctor's profession was born from shyness.

exploreAction.targetName: Laennec's 1819 treatise on mediate auscultation
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Laennec described the sounds of the chest — crackles, murmurs, friction — and correlated them with autopsies to build a diagnostic language. He died at 45 of tuberculosis, the very disease he'd learned to hear. The tube that let doctors listen to the body's complaints.

name: Endoscopy (1806-68)
teaser: Philipp Bozzini's 'Lichtleiter' — a candle in a tube with mirrors — was the first endoscope, described in 1806. Adolf Kussmaul swallowed a sword-swallower's technique to peer into a stomach with a rigid tube in 1868. A century of refinement (flexible fibers, cameras, LEDs) made the modern endoscope, which now inspects nearly every human passage.

exploreAction.targetName: The history of endoscopy from candlelight to capsule cameras
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Kussmaul, inspired by watching a sword swallower, passed a rigid tube into a patient's stomach — by torchlight. Then the fiber-optic revolution of the 1960s and the capsule camera that you swallow like a pill. From candles to cameras: 200 years of looking inside.

name: Ether Anesthesia (1846)
teaser: William Morton, a Boston dentist, publicly demonstrated ether anesthesia at the Massachusetts General Hospital in October 1846 — 'Gentlemen, this is no humbug,' said the surgeon John Collins Warren. The news circled the globe in months. Surgery changed from a screaming ordeal to a silent procedure in a single afternoon.

exploreAction.targetName: The Ether Day demonstration at MGH
exploreAction.instruction: Read about October 16, 1846: the patient Gilbert Abbott, the tumor removal, the crowd of skeptical surgeons. Then the ugly credit war — Crawford Long, Horace Wells, Charles Jackson all claimed priority. The ether dome still stands in Boston, a shrine to the day pain stopped being inevitable.

name: Nitroglycerin for Angina (1870s)
teaser: Workers who handled nitroglycerin at dynamite plants complained of pounding headaches — and doctors noticed something else: it relieved their chest pain. Nitroglycerin became the first effective treatment for angina, and it still is. Alfred Nobel, who invented dynamite from nitroglycerin, was prescribed it for his own heart.

exploreAction.targetName: The story of dynamite workers and the angina cure
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Murrell, a London physician, read about the dynamite workers' headaches and chest-pain relief, then prescribed dilute nitroglycerin to angina patients with dramatic effect. It remains the emergency drug of choice 150 years later. And yes — Nobel took it for his heart, and it worked.

name: Adrenaline (1901)
teaser: Jokichi Takamine isolated and crystallized adrenaline from cow adrenal glands in 1901 — the first hormone ever purified, and the first drug to act on a specific target. It opened endocrinology as a science. Today it's the epinephrine auto-injector that stops allergic reactions — the same molecule, in a pen.

exploreAction.targetName: Takamine's 1901 isolation of adrenaline
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Takamine, a Japanese chemist working in the US, extracted the 'active principle' of the adrenal gland, patented it, and watched it launch the pharmaceutical industry's hormone era. Then trace it to the EpiPen: the discovery that a single molecule can reboot a failing body.

name: Thyroid Extract (1891)
teaser: George Murray injected sheep thyroid extract into a woman dying of myxedema — severe hypothyroidism — and she recovered within months. It was the first replacement therapy for a hormone deficiency, and it proved that the thyroid's product was essential to life. Endocrinology, as a treatment, began here.

exploreAction.targetName: Murray's 1891 thyroid extract treatment
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Murray, a Manchester physician, connected cretinism and myxedema to thyroid failure, then tried gland extract — the first organotherapy. The patient lived another 28 years. The leap from 'the gland is broken' to 'replace its product' founded modern hormone therapy.

name: Cortisone (1949)
teaser: Philip Hench watched a bedridden rheumatoid arthritis patient nearly dance out of the hospital days after receiving 'Compound E' — cortisone. The Merck team had spent years extracting the hormone from cattle bile. The 1950 announcement made front pages; the Nobel followed within months. It was the first 'miracle drug' of the postwar era.

exploreAction.targetName: The 1949 cortisone announcement at Mayo Clinic
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Hench, a rheumatologist, and Kendall, a chemist, collaborated across departments, and how the first 14 patients responded within days. Then the sobering follow-up: cortisone's side effects and the realization that it treats inflammation, not the disease. The miracle drug that taught medicine about steroid power and limits.
